title: Workflow Mapping - Swimlane
subtitle: Diagram
useWhen: Work keeps falling through the cracks at the same points. Two people think someone else owns the handoff. Processes that should be smooth have invisible gaps that only become visible when something goes wrong.
howToUse: A Swimlane diagram maps a process across multiple roles or departments, with each role occupying its own horizontal lane. Every action in the process is placed in the lane of the person responsible. Handoffs where work moves from one lane to another, become immediately visible. The diagram reveals where delays, duplications, and accountability gaps cluster. For complex multi-team processes, it is the clearest way to see the whole picture at once. AI can generate swimlane descriptions and identify the highest-risk handoffs when given process context.
steps: Map each role involved in the process as a separate lane. 2. Mark every handoff explicitly, the arrows between lanes are where most failures happen.
Look for lanes with the most incoming arrows, that person is your bottleneck.

After mapping, identify the one handoff that fails most often and redesign it first. See exactly where handoffs break before they break again A swimlane diagram shows you where the handoff breaks, not why. If a lane has too many incoming arrows, the fix is rarely "work harder", it's usually a workload or ownership problem the diagram alone won't solve.
origin: Process improvement methodology — swimlane diagrams formalised 1940s onwards
promptBody:
Act as a process improvement consultant specialising in workflow mapping.
Process to map       :  [NAME AND DESCRIBE THE PROCESS END TO END]
Roles involved         :  [LIST ALL PEOPLE OR TEAMS WHO TOUCH THIS PROCESS]
Known pain points :  [WHERE THINGS GO WRONG OR SLOW DOWN]
Map this process as a text-based Swimlane diagram:
Format                       :  ROLE | Step description | Output / Handoff to
After the map:
1.Identify the 3 highest-risk handoff points
2.Name the role that is the biggest bottleneck
3.Identify any steps that add no value and could be removed
4.Suggest one redesign that would most improve flow
Flag any step where accountability is shared between two lanes, 
those are your highest failure risk points.

proTip:
Shared accountability between lanes is the number one predictor of process failure. When
two roles both touch a step, both assume the other is checking it. The fix is always the
same: assign one person as Accountable (using RACI) and make the handoff explicit with a
defined output format and a confirmation step.
